newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK stocks surge on handover confidence.
newsitem.headline: HK stocks surge on handover confidence.

text.p: The death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping proved no hurdle for Hong Kong stocks, which staged a big rally on Thursday on confidence that Hong Kong's transition to Chinese rule would be largely unaffected.
"This does not affect anything whatsoever," said Jake van der Kamp, investment strategist at HG Asia.
"That is the tribute to the man -- that he organised all this in his life so that when he died it would go swiftly," he said.
China announced late on Wednesday that Deng had died of complications from Parkinson's disease and a lung infection.
After an opening fall of 92 points, Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index surged 305.01 points, or 2.33 percent, to 13,411.33.
"It proved to be one of the most discounted events in Hong Kong's recent political history," said Pauline Gately, regional strategist at Merrill Lynch.

"We don't think there is going to be any change to the recipe of "one-country, two-systems". Deng Xiaoping was the architect but it is widely acknowledged that it is recognised as the approach that best serves China's interests," she added.
Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule at midnight June 30. China has pledged that the territory will have a high degree of autonomy for 50 years after the transition.
Expectations of a smooth transition have supported the Hang Seng Index in the past, driving it to an all-time high of 14,004.93 on January 16. Since then, stocks have consolidated.

"The market has been sluggish for almost two months so a lot of selling pressure has been removed. I expect the market to gain momentum," said Peter So, deputy head of research at Schroder Securities.
Alex Tang, head of research at Yamaichi International, said investors had been waiting for an entry point into the market.
"The market should be able to challenge the previous high of 14,004 very, very soon. Probably in the early part of March we will be back at the 14,000 level again," he said.
Many analysts said they did not expect any significant changes in policy in China following Deng's death.
"In the end I think it will be business as usual and the underlying reforms that Deng had put into place will not be undone," said Andrew Fernow, director of research at Vickers Ballas.
"The collective leadership in China is rather stable and the people in charge of the Communist Party have pretty secure backing from the military and bureaucracy," he added.
Van der Kamp dismissed fears that there would be a power struggle following Deng's death.
"That, the market is telling us, and the Chinese markets as well, is not going to be the case," he said.
In Shenzhen, the foreign-currency B-share index rose 1.78 points, or 1.26 percent, to 143.53 but the domestic A-share index fell 7.54 points, or 2.11 percent, to 350.59.
In Shanghai, the B-share index fell 0.455 points, or 0.70 percent, to 64.675 but the A-share index added 2.781, or 0.28 percent, to 1,007.731.
Some analysts sounded a note of caution, however.

"The designate for Chief Executive, Tung Chee-hwa, has waffled a little bit on some important issues that affect the people of Hong Kong so people are not as reassured that he will exert strong leadership," said Fernow.

"Until he demonstrates that he can handle the job of Chief Executive, I think some people may worry that Beijing's hand in running Hong Kong will be heavy-handed and that will perhaps affect the outlook for Hong Kong."
But Fernow said once Tung and China "reassure the people of Hong Kong that their intentions are good and there won't be much change", confidence would be restored to the market.
